answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: The line comes from Wharton's dramatic monologue “Vesalius in Zante (1564),” spoken by the dying anatomist Andreas Vesalius as he reflects on his scientific legacy — first printed in The North American Review in November 1902 and later collected in her verse volume Artemis to Actæon (1909).

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: The North American Review, vol. 175, November 1902, p. 631
Artemis to Actæon, and Other Verses (New York: Charles Scribner's Sons, 1909), pp. 14–23

source.excerpt:
For thus I read the meaning of this end:
There are two ways of spreading light: to be
The candle or the mirror that reflects it.
I let my wick burn out—there yet remains
To spread an answering surface to the flame
That others kindle.
trail: First appeared in The North American Review, November 1902 ↗, where the poem was originally titled “Vesalius in Zante (1564).”
Collected seven years later in Wharton's book of verse, Artemis to Actæon, and Other Verses ↗ (Scribner's, 1909).
The full poem, including the candle/mirror lines in context, is preserved at Wikisource ↗.
The line's attribution to Wharton and this exact source is corroborated by Wikiquote's Edith Wharton page ↗, which cites the same North American Review, November 1902, p. 631.

source.excerptNote: Spoken in the poem's closing lines by the dying Vesalius, reconciling himself to the fact that his own work is finished but that others will carry its light forward.

author.name: Edith Wharton
author.heading: About Edith Wharton
author.bio: Best known for novels like The Age of Innocence and The House of Mirth, Wharton was also a serious poet whose verse appeared in major literary magazines. “Vesalius in Zante” is a dramatic monologue in blank verse imagining the last thoughts of the Renaissance anatomist Andreas Vesalius.

context.heading: A dying scientist's consolation
lead: In Wharton's poem, the speaker is the Renaissance anatomist Andreas Vesalius, shipwrecked and dying on the Greek island of Zante while returning from a pilgrimage to Jerusalem. Looking back on a career of groundbreaking (and controversial) work in human dissection, he reconciles himself to the fact that his own candle has burned down — but that his discoveries will go on being reflected and carried forward by the scientists who follow him.

The candle/mirror image resonated well beyond the poem's original context and today circulates almost entirely as a standalone inspirational quotation, most often with no mention of Vesalius or the poem it comes from.
context.pull: I let my wick burn out—there yet remains / To spread an answering surface to the flame / That others kindle.
